# Results — Study 474 (Accelerator Oscillator)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Bill Williams' claim — **acceleration
leads price: two consecutive rising AC bars above zero forecast continuation up** — encoded as a
mechanical rule. AC = AO − SMA5(AO), where AO = SMA5(median) − SMA34(median); all windows trailing
(closed-bar, no look-ahead). A long fires when AC[t] > AC[t−1] > AC[t−2] and AC[t] > 0, entered at
the **next close** (one documented lag), and we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline &
deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **2131** mechanical two-green-bars-above-zero turn-ups pooled across the 5 tapes |
| AC params | AO = SMA5(median) − SMA34(median); AC = AO − SMA5(AO); all trailing |
| Timing / costs | AC read on close of *t*; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per entry |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument momentum study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — AC turn-up vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch AC-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = AC − random.

| horizon | n | AC | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (AC−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 2126 | +11.0 bps | 56% | +2.16 | +10.4 bps | **+0.5 bps** | +9.0 bps | +0.07 | 0.945 |
| 10-day | 2126 | +45.5 bps | 60% | +6.17 | +26.5 bps | **+19.0 bps** | +43.5 bps | +1.73 | 0.083 |
| 20-day | 2121 | +88.2 bps | 63% | +6.50 | +80.1 bps | **+8.1 bps** | +86.2 bps | +0.54 | 0.591 |
| 60-day | 2111 | +252.1 bps | 68% | +7.13 | +256.1 bps | **−4.0 bps** | +250.1 bps | −0.16 | 0.874 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero looks spectacular (**+6.50** at 20 days,
**+7.13** at 60) — but that is **pure beta**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting index inherit
the drift. Against the **drift-matched random baseline**, the AC turn-up is essentially flat at
every horizon (Δ = +0.5 / +19.0 / +8.1 / −4.0 bps). The AC-minus-random difference **never clears
the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar** (best is Welch *t* = +1.73 at 10 days, *p* = 0.083 — and it *reverses* to
−0.16 at 60 days). Acceleration does not forecast price beyond the drift any dip/dump-buy inherits.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — no coherent cross-sectional edge

| ticker | entries | AC | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (AC−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 422 | +77.9 bps | +3.03 | +84.4 bps | **−6.5 bps** |
| QQQ | 409 | +120.3 bps | +3.61 | +102.9 bps | **+17.4 bps** |
| IWM | 433 | +72.6 bps | +2.04 | +40.6 bps | **+32.0 bps** |
| DIA | 433 | +78.1 bps | +3.31 | +54.4 bps | **+23.6 bps** |
| GLD | 434 | +93.8 bps | +3.16 | +119.7 bps | **−25.9 bps** |

The deltas straddle zero (positive in 3 of 5, negative in 2) with no sign of a stable edge: AC beats
random on IWM/DIA/QQQ by a little, *loses* on SPY and GLD. Pooled it washes out to +8.1 bps at *t* =
+0.54 — the hallmark of relabelled drift, not a forecasting signal.

## Timing placebo — rotate the AC series, nothing changes

The decisive "does the AC-to-price timing matter?" test: keep the AC values **exactly** (same bars,
same two-green-bars run structure) but circularly **rotate** the AC series relative to price by a
random offset, so its alignment with forward returns is meaningless. If acceleration genuinely
*leads* price, the rotation would collapse the result.

| test | observed AC-up 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY rotated-AC | +77.9 bps | **0.886** | 500 |

**89% of rotated-AC series match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.886). The AC's alignment with price
carries no information — a meaningless time-shift does just as well. "Acceleration leads price" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real acceleration

On a deterministic tape with *planted* upward-accelerating episodes (knob `edge`), the same
two-green-bars-above-zero rule behaves exactly as it must — so the flat real-tape result is a genuine
"nothing there", not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | AC | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no acceleration) | 303 | −21.7 bps | 46% | −0.67 |
| **0.80** (real planted acceleration) | 298 | +272.0 bps | 62% | **+5.33** |

With no planted acceleration the control sits at *t* ≈ 0 (no false positive); a real planted
acceleration episode lights up at *t* = +5.33 with a 62% win-rate. The detector is live.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The AC turn-up does **not** beat a drift-matched random baseline
  (AC − random = +0.5 / +19.0 / +8.1 / −4.0 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the AC-vs-random Welch *t* never
  clears 2, best +1.73 at 10 days, *p* = 0.083, and reverses to −0.16 by 60 days). The impressive
  one-sample *t*'s (20-day +6.50, 60-day +7.13) are pure beta — the upward drift of long equity indices.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no residual edge once the drift you were always getting is
  removed, and costs only deepen the hole. The same drift is captured more cheaply and more fully by
  holding the index; the AC rule trades less and pays costs on each entry, dominating nothing. No
  capacity question because there is no edge to scale.
- **"Does acceleration forecast price"? — BUSTED.** The rotated-AC placebo leaves the result intact
  (*p* = 0.886): a meaningless time-shift of the AC series does as well as the real alignment, so the
  acceleration-to-price timing carries no forecasting information. The Accelerator Oscillator is a
  re-described second derivative of past price, not a forecast.
